title: Arthur Douillard (@Ar_Douillard)
clean_title: The legacy of the LeCun lab at NYU in deep learning
summary:
The LeCun “mafia” from NYU is honestly pretty incredible. Just look up what everyone from that lab and time did since then
Quoting @ylecun
The tensor engine was first implemented inside SN3 (before it was called Lush) in 1992 at Bell Labs by Léon Bottom and me.
The naming convention has survived to this day in PyTorch and other libraries.
The naming of the tensor operations was reused in EBlearn (C++ deep learning library written by Pierre Sermanet and me, with some help from @soumithchintala).
It was recycled in Torch5 and Torch7, which was written largely by Ronan Collobert, and my students Clément Farabet, and @koraykv ). Clément and Koray had been brought up on Lush (the open version of SN) and knew the nomenclature.
Then, Soumith used the same conventions in PyTorch.

title: Arthur Douillard (@Ar_Douillard)
clean_title: Decoupled DiLoCo enables resilient AI training across distant datacenters
summary:
Decoupled DiLoCo by @Ar_Douillard and @GoogleDeepMind and Research looks incredible
Decoupled DiLoCo lets you train frontier models across distant datacenters without the usual bandwidth tax or sync bottlenecks
• ~235x less network bandwidth needed between datacenters
• Kept 88% of training useful when hardware was failing constantly. The old approach dropped to 27%
• Final model quality basically identical (64.1% vs 64.4%)
• Trained a 12B model across 4 US regions over regular internet-grade connections, 20x faster than the traditional method
Today frontier training today requires thousands of identical chips locked in sync inside a single mega data center
Decoupled DiLoCo changes that. Training runs across separate islands of compute that keep learning even when one fails, can mix hardware generations in the same run, and don't need custom cross datacenter fiber.
That means compute anywhere on Earth becomes useful, older chips stay on the frontier roster instead of aging out, and open-source and smaller labs finally have a real path to pool distributed compute and compete at scale. The biggest bottleneck on the next generation of AI has been physical power, fiber, floor space in one building. This is the blueprint for decoupling AI progress from that constraint.
Also early in thought here but I think @doublezero / @Austin_Federa's private fiber lines will be really important for AI training/inference in the future building on their crypto infra angle today.
If you can train this models using the public internet with Decoupled Diloco imagine using private fiber lines. I'd be curious how much this improves the situation and what the metrics are side by side.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGmh4IwWUAAEE-0.jpg
Quoting @Ar_Douillard
The DiLoCo team at Google DeepMind and Google Research is proud to release Decoupled DiLoCo, the next frontier for resilient AI pre-training.
Decoupled DiLoCo enables training with datacenters across the world, using heterogeneous hardware, and never halting the system despite hardware failures.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HGmTt3CXQAAv2DG.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/tweet_video/HGmTt3CXQAAv2DG.mp4
clean_summary:
Decoupled DiLoCo by @Ar_Douillard and @GoogleDeepMind looks incredible. It allows training frontier models across distant datacenters without the usual bandwidth tax or synchronization bottlenecks.

This approach requires approximately 235 times less network bandwidth between datacenters and retains 88% of training usefulness even when hardware is failing, compared to just 27% with the old method. The final model quality remains nearly identical (64.1% vs 64.4%), and a 12B model was trained across four US regions over regular internet-grade connections, achieving speeds 20 times faster than traditional methods.

Decoupled DiLoCo changes the landscape of AI training by enabling runs across separate compute islands that continue learning despite failures, allowing for mixed hardware generations in the same run, and eliminating the need for custom cross-datacenter fiber. This advancement means that compute resources anywhere on Earth can be utilized, older chips can remain relevant, and smaller labs can compete at scale, breaking the physical constraints that have limited AI progress. Additionally, private fiber lines may further enhance AI training and inference capabilities.
